claim: Medical professionals in the northeast region of Brazil reported a surge in the number of children born with microcephaly in late 2015, with an increase of 265% in the number of cases during 2015–2016.
source: In late 2015, medical professionals in the northeast region of Brazil reported a surge in the number of children born with microcephaly, with an increase of 265% in the number of cases during 2015–2016 (Microcephaly Epidemic Research Group, 2016; Kleber de Oliveira et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Microcephaly Epidemic Research Group, 2016; Kleber de Oliveira et al., 2016).

claim: Infants born with microcephaly during the Zika outbreak had a constellation of clinical presentations that became known as Congenital Zika Syndrome (CZS), including skull deformation, abnormally small cerebral cortices, and retinal scarring.
source: Infants born with microcephaly during the Zika outbreak also had a constellation of clinical presentations that ultimately became known as Congenital Zika Syndrome (CZS): skull deformation, abnormally small cerebral cortices, and retinal scarring, among others (Broussard et al., 2018; Moore et al., 2017; Musso et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Broussard et al., 2018; Moore et al., 2017; Musso et al., 2019).

claim: Children with CZS have continued to develop additional health issues including visual impairment, increased risk for autism, atypical motor development, increased risk for cerebral palsy, and poor sleep quality.
source: Clinicians have identified additional health issues as these children have continued to grow and develop (Wheeler et al., 2018; Cardoso et al., 2019), including visual impairment (Ventura et al., 2017), increased risk for autism (Vianna et al., 2018), atypical motor development, increased risk for cerebral palsy (Marques et al., 2019), and poor sleep quality (Pinato et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research (Wheeler et al., 2018; Cardoso et al., 2019; Ventura et al., 2017; Vianna et al., 2018; Marques et al., 2019; Pinato et al., 2018).

claim: Up to 50% of children born to mothers infected with Zika virus during pregnancy exhibit anatomical or behavioral abnormalities.
source: Further screening has identified cases where children not diagnosed with CZS at birth exhibit CZS by their first birthday; up to 50% of children born to mothers infected with Zika virus during pregnancy infection exhibit anatomical or behavioral abnormalities (Cardoso et al., 2019; Wheeler, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Cardoso et al., 2019; Wheeler, 2018).

claim: ZIKV may use AXL, a tyrosine kinase receptor important in modulating the innate immune system, to enter the brain.
source: The neurotropism of the virus may result from ZIKV using AXL, a tyrosine kinase receptor important in modulating the innate immune system (Rothlin et al., 2007; Hafizi and Dahlbäck, 2006), to enter the brain (Meertens et al., 2017; Rossi et al., 2020; Nowakowski et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Rothlin et al., 2007; Hafizi and Dahlbäck, 2006; Meertens et al., 2017; Rossi et al., 2020; Nowakowski et al., 2016).

claim: AXL is highly expressed in radial glia, endothelial cells, microglia, and astrocytes in the developing human cortex.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing analyses have demonstrated that AXL is highly expressed in radial glia, endothelial cells, microglia, and astrocytes in the developing human cortex (Nowakowski et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Nowakowski et al., 2016).

claim: After breaching the placental–fetal barrier, ZIKV infects radial glial cells.
source: After breaching the placental–fetal barrier, ZIKV infects radial glial cells.
evidence: The claim is stated as an established fact in the manuscript, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Radial glia cells undergo symmetric and asymmetric cell division to generate the neurons that populate the cerebral cortex.
source: Radial glia cells undergo symmetric and asymmetric cell division to generate the neurons that populate the cerebral cortex (Anthony et al., 2004; Falk and Götz, 2017), and the disruption of this process may ultimately lead to decreased neuronal numbers resulting in microcephaly.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Anthony et al., 2004; Falk and Götz, 2017).

claim: Disruption of radial glia cell division may ultimately lead to decreased neuronal numbers resulting in microcephaly.
source: Radial glia cells undergo symmetric and asymmetric cell division to generate the neurons that populate the cerebral cortex (Anthony et al., 2004; Falk and Götz, 2017), and the disruption of this process may ultimately lead to decreased neuronal numbers resulting in microcephaly.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the role of radial glia in neurogenesis.

claim: Once infected, microglia and astrocytes can propagate and spread ZIKV through the brain, maintaining a high viral load in the brain over time.
source: Although ZIKV might not be cytotoxic for microglia and astrocytes initially, once infected, these cells can propagate and spread the virus through the brain, maintaining a high viral load in the brain over time (Muffat et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Muffat et al., 2018).

claim: Microglia play a critical role in neural development by promoting neuronal survival via release of neurotrophic factors, phagocytosing immature neurons that fail to form proper neuronal circuits, and removing redundant or dysfunctional synapses.
source: They also play a critical role in neural development by promoting neuronal survival via release of neurotrophic factors to support neuronal circuit formation, phagocytosing immature neurons that fail to form proper neuronal circuits, and removing redundant or dysfunctional synapses in the developing brain (Thion et al., 2018; Reemst et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Thion et al., 2018; Reemst et al., 2016).

claim: During the late stages of brain development and after birth, glial cells develop and spread through the nervous system, constituting at least half of the cellular population within the brain.
source: During the late stages of brain development and after birth, glial cells develop and spread through the nervous system, constituting at least half of the cellular population within the brain (Zuchero and Barres, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Zuchero and Barres, 2015).

claim: Congenitally acquired ZIKV infects glial precursor cells, impairing their distribution in the brain and leading to reduced and delayed myelination.
source: Congenitally acquired ZIKV has been shown to infect glial precursor cells, impairing their distribution in the brain, leading to reduced and delayed myelination (Chimelli and Avvad-Portari, 2018), ultimately contributing to neuroinflammation and microcephaly.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Chimelli and Avvad-Portari, 2018).

claim: Nonhuman primate models of ZIKV infection can bridge the translational divide between rodent models and humans.
source: Nonhuman primate (NHP) models of ZIKV infection have been established and are able to bridge the translational divide between rodent models and humans (Nguyen et al., 2017; Coffey et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Nguyen et al., 2017; Coffey et al., 2018).

claim: Adult mouse models of ZIKV must be immunocompromised or genetically modified.
source: Rodent models have significant limitations including the fact that adult mouse models of ZIKV must be immunocompromised or genetically modified (e.g., Winkler and Peterson, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Winkler and Peterson, 2018).

claim: Fetal and neonatal wild-type mice show some susceptibility to ZIKV infection but must be directly exposed to the virus and are not a good model for vertical transmission.
source: Fetal and neonatal wild-type mice do show some susceptibility to ZIKV infection, but they must be directly exposed to the virus, either through intracerebroventricular, intraperitoneal, or intra-amniotic (IA) inoculation, and as such are not a good model for vertical transmission of ZIKV from infected mothers to fetuses (e.g., Paul et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Paul et al., 2018).

claim: The extent to which certain cortical regions are homologous in rodents and primates is not clear.
source: In addition, the most severe symptoms of CZS include dysfunction in the neocortex, especially the prefrontal cortex (PFC), and the extent to which certain cortical regions are homologous in rodents and primates is not clear (Laubach et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Laubach et al., 2018).

claim: NHP gestational development is similar to humans in its extended duration, the prevalence of singleton pregnancies, and the structure of the placenta.
source: NHPs gestational development is also similar to humans, including its extended duration (relative to rodents), the prevalence of singleton pregnancies (rather than litters), and the structure of the placenta (Carter, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Carter, 2007).

claim: The anatomical development and organization of the brain proceed along a similar path in humans and NHPs.
source: The anatomical development and organization of the brain also proceed along a similar path in humans and NHPs (Workman et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Workman et al., 2013).

claim: Pregnant NHPs do not need to be immunocompromised to be infected with ZIKV, experience viremia, and demonstrate transplacental transmission of the virus to the fetus.
source: Similar to humans, pregnant NHPs do not need to be immunocompromised to be infected with ZIKV, experience viremia, and demonstrate transplacental transmission of the virus to the fetus (Koide et al., 2016; Dudley et al., 2016; Morrison and Diamond, 2017; Coffey et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Koide et al., 2016; Dudley et al., 2016; Morrison and Diamond, 2017; Coffey et al., 2017).

claim: Previous studies of ZIKV-exposed fetal and infant macaques have identified pathological features including calcifications, abnormal gliosis, and white matter hypoplasia, although none had evidence of microcephaly.
source: Although none had evidence of microcephaly, previous studies of ZIKV-exposed fetal and infant macaques have identified a number of pathological features, including calcifications, abnormal gliosis, and white matter hypoplasia (Coffey et al., 2018; Mavigner et al., 2018; Adams Waldorf et al., 2018; Adams Waldorf et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Coffey et al., 2018; Mavigner et al., 2018; Adams Waldorf et al., 2018; Adams Waldorf et al., 2016).

claim: Studies employing immunohistochemical analysis identified loss of neural precursors, reduced neurogenesis, gliosis, and increased apoptosis in different brain regions of ZIKV-exposed macaques.
source: Studies that employed immunohistochemical (IHC) analysis also identified loss of neural precursors, reduced neurogenesis, gliosis, and increased apoptosis in different brain regions (Coffey et al., 2018; Mavigner et al., 2018; Adams Waldorf et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Coffey et al., 2018; Mavigner et al., 2018; Adams Waldorf et al., 2018).

claim: Formalin fixation and paraffin embedding can mask epitopes, reduce antigenicity, and make it challenging to understand the impact of infection on the whole brain.
source: Neuroanatomical evaluations in these studies have adopted approaches that are standard for pathologic analyses, insofar as they typically evaluate small areas of brain tissue and use formalin fixation and paraffin embedding, procedures that can mask epitopes, reduce antigenicity, and make it challenging to understand the impact of infection on the whole brain (Cinar et al., 2006; Jones and Hartman, 1978).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Cinar et al., 2006; Jones and Hartman, 1978).

claim: The present study builds upon a previously described macaque model of CZS in which fetuses were inoculated with ZIKV via the IA route, mothers were concurrently inoculated with ZIKV intravenously, and fetuses were harvested at the end of gestation.
source: The present study builds upon a previously described macaque model of CZS in which, to assure fetal infection at a defined time of gestation, fetuses were inoculated with ZIKV via the IA routes, mothers were concurrently inoculated with ZIKV intravenously (IV), and fetuses were harvested at the end of gestation (Coffey et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Coffey et al., 2018).

claim: IHC confocal microscopy revealed the presence of clusters of reactive glia within Area 46 of the PFC from ZIKV+ animals, but not in the controls.
source: IHC confocal microscopy revealed the presence of clusters of reactive glia within Area 46 of the PFC from ZIKV+ animals, but not in the controls (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from immunohistochemical confocal microscopy and referenced in Figure 1A, B.

claim: Abnormal clusters of Iba1+ microglia also express the lysosomal marker CD68 in the ZIKV-infected animals.
source: Multiple labeling fluorescent microscopy allowed us to visualize that abnormal clusters of Iba1+ microglia which also express the lysosomal marker CD68 in the ZIKV-infected animals (Figure 1C–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from multiple labeling fluorescent microscopy and referenced in Figure 1C–G.

claim: CD68 levels are substantially upregulated in microglia during inflammatory processes and are thought to be involved in active phagocytosis.
source: CD68 levels are known to be substantially upregulated in microglia during inflammatory processes and are thought to be involved in active phagocytosis (Jurga et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Jurga et al., 2020).

claim: Clusters of amoeboid-shaped microglia within Area 46 are directly engulfing neuronal debris in the ZIKV-infected monkeys.
source: We also observed that clusters of amoeboid-shaped microglia within Area 46, are directly engulfing neuronal debris in the ZIKV-infected monkeys (Figure 1H, I; 3D reconstruction: Figure 1J, K).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from microscopy and 3D reconstruction, referenced in Figure 1H, I, J, K.

claim: ZIKV envelope protein was observed within Area 46 of all the infected animals, with detection of viral protein inside clusters of microglia, but not astrocytes.
source: Interestingly, we observed the presence of ZIKV envelope protein within Area 46 of all the infected animals, with detection of viral protein inside clusters of microglia, but not astrocytes (GFAP, Figures 2A–G and 3D reconstruction: Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from immunohistochemistry and 3D reconstruction, referenced in Figures 2A–G and Figure 2H.

claim: ZIKV+ cells are thought to be in a direct process of phagocytosis, a common event occurring during viral encephalitis.
source: As shown in Figure 2I, J, these ZIKV+ cells are thought to be in a direct process of phagocytosis, a common event occurring during viral encephalitis (Chhatbar and Prinz, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from microscopy (Figure 2I, J) and a citation to published research (Chhatbar and Prinz, 2021).

claim: ZIKV+ cells were surrounded and in direct contact with reactive microglia also expressing CD68.
source: While we could not detect the expression of other proteins in the ZIKV+ cells, they were surrounded and in direct contact with reactive microglia also expressing CD68, as shown in Figure 2K, L.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from microscopy, referenced in Figure 2K, L.

claim: Gyrification of the occipital lobe was significantly reduced in ZIKV-infected animals as compared with control animals.
source: Gyrification of the occipital lobe was significantly reduced in ZIKV-infected animals as compared with control animals (t4 = 3.33, p = 0.029; d = 2.72) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data and referenced in Figure 3B.

claim: The occipital lobes from ZIKV animals had a significantly higher proportion of white matter and lower proportion of gray matter than the control animals.
source: However, differences between the proportions of white and gray matter varied by condition. The occipital lobes from ZIKV animals had a significantly higher proportion of white matter and lower proportion of gray matter than the control animals (t4 = 2.93, p = 0.043; d = 2.39; because the occipital lobe included only gray and white matter, the proportions are inverses of each other and the statistics identical) (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data and referenced in Figure 3C.

claim: Cortical thickness in Area 17 did not differ significantly between ZIKV and control subjects, although all the data points for the ZIKV group were below the mean of the control group.
source: Cortical thickness in that area did not differ significantly between ZIKV and control subjects (t4 = 1.42, p = 0.230; d = 1.16; Figure 3A), although all the data points for the ZIKV group were below the mean of the control group, suggesting the possibility of cortical thinning within the primary visual cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data and referenced in Figure 3A.

claim: There was no difference between ZIKV and control animals in the gyrification of the frontal lobes.
source: There was no difference between ZIKV and control animals in the gyrification of the frontal lobes (t4 = 0.56, p = 0.60; d = 0.46) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data and referenced in Figure 3B.

claim: There were no significant differences between cortical thickness in Area 46 of ZIKV and control animals.
source: There were no significant differences between cortical thickness in Area 17 (Figure 4A) and in Area 46 (Figure 4B) of ZIKV and control animals (t4 = 0.57, p = 0.60; d = 0.46; Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data and referenced in Figure 4B.

claim: ZIKV infection did not cause gross morphological changes to frontal cortex during development.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that ZIKV infection did not cause gross morphological changes to frontal cortex during development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the absence of significant differences in multiple measurements of frontal cortex structure.

claim: There was not a difference in cortical thickness between the Zika and control animals in Area 4 (primary motor cortex).
source: There was not a difference in cortical thickness between the Zika and control animals in Area 4 (t4 = 0.80, p = 0.47; d = 0.65; MeanZIKV = 2427.76 μm, SDZIKV = 95.64 μm; MeanControl = 2361.72 μm, SDControl = 106.62 μm).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data.

claim: There were no differences between the ZIKV and control groups in the volumes of the amygdala and hippocampus.
source: There were no differences between the ZIKV and control groups in the volumes of the amygdala, hippocampus. Amygdala: t4 = 0.095, p = 0.93; d = 0.078; MeanZika = 79.85 mm3, SDZika = 3.88 mm3; MeanControl = 79.28 mm3, SDControl = 9.45 mm3. Hippocampus: t4 = 0.58, p = 0.59; d = 0.47; MeanZika = 135.82 mm3, SDZika = 10.65 mm3; MeanControl = 143.97 mm3, SDControl = 21.84 mm3.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data.

claim: There were no group differences between the ZIKV and control animals in the volume of their optic tracts.
source: There were no group differences between the ZIKV and control animals in the volume of their optic tracts: t4 = 1.061, p = 0.35; d = 0.87; MeanZika = 31.24 mm3, SDZika = 6.54 mm3; MeanControl = 25.09 mm3, SDControl = 7.62 mm3.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data.

claim: The three-dimensional space glia occupy, especially microglia, change constantly because these cells are highly dynamic and retract and expand their processes in response to subtle changes in the surrounding environment.
source: The three-dimensional space glia occupy, especially microglia, change constantly, because these cells are highly dynamic and retract and expand their processes in response to subtle changes in the surrounding environment.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific knowledge about microglial dynamics.

claim: Glial cells have a strong form-to-function mapping and investigating morphological alterations in these cells allows inferences about their activation state and their inflammatory status across different brain regions.
source: Several studies have shown that glial cells have a strong form-to-function mapping and investigating morphological alterations in these cells allows inferences about their activation state and their inflammatory status across different brain regions (Karperien et al., 2013; Morrison and Filosa, 2013; Young and Morrison, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Karperien et al., 2013; Morrison and Filosa, 2013; Young and Morrison, 2018).

claim: In Area 17, there were no significant differences in microglia cell body size between ZIKV-infected and control animals.
source: Analysis of the microglia in Area 17 revealed no significant differences in the cell body size (t4 = 0.36, p = 0.74; d = 0.29; Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data and referenced in Figure 5C.

claim: In Area 17, the whole cell volumes of microglia were marginally smaller in ZIKV-infected animals than in control animals with a very large effect size.
source: The whole cell volumes were marginally smaller in ZIKV-infected animals than in control animals and while the p value did not reach conventional levels of significance, the effect size was very large (t4 = 2.71, p = 0.054; d = 2.11; Figure 5D)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data and referenced in Figure 5D.

claim: In Area 17, there were no group differences in the number of terminal points of microglia between ZIKV-infected and control animals.
source: There were no group differences in the number of terminal points (t4 = 0.83, p = 0.45; d = 0.68; Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data and referenced in Figure 5E.

claim: In Area 46, there were no significant differences between the cell body size of microglia in ZIKV-infected compared to control animals.
source: In contrast, while there were no significant differences between the cell body size of microglia in Area 46 of ZIKV-infected compared to control animals (t4 = 2.07, p = 0.11; d = 1.69; Figure 5M), ZIKV-infected animals, compared to controls, had significantly smaller whole cell volumes (t4 = 9.41, p < 0.001; d = 7.68; Figure 5N) and significantly fewer terminal points (t4 = 4.18, p = 0.01; d = 3.41; Figure 5O).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data and referenced in Figure 5M.

claim: In Area 46, ZIKV-infected animals had significantly smaller microglia whole cell volumes compared to controls.
source: In contrast, while there were no significant differences between the cell body size of microglia in Area 46 of ZIKV-infected compared to control animals (t4 = 2.07, p = 0.11; d = 1.69; Figure 5M), ZIKV-infected animals, compared to controls, had significantly smaller whole cell volumes (t4 = 9.41, p < 0.001; d = 7.68; Figure 5N) and significantly fewer terminal points (t4 = 4.18, p = 0.01; d = 3.41; Figure 5O).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data and referenced in Figure 5N.

claim: In Area 46, ZIKV-infected animals had significantly fewer microglia terminal points compared to controls.
source: In contrast, while there were no significant differences between the cell body size of microglia in Area 46 of ZIKV-infected compared to control animals (t4 = 2.07, p = 0.11; d = 1.69; Figure 5M), ZIKV-infected animals, compared to controls, had significantly smaller whole cell volumes (t4 = 9.41, p < 0.001; d = 7.68; Figure 5N) and significantly fewer terminal points (t4 = 4.18, p = 0.01; d = 3.41; Figure 5O).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data and referenced in Figure 5O.

claim: The smaller whole cell volumes and fewer terminal points of microglia in Area 46 suggest that the microglia were in their activated state in frontal cortex.
source: The smaller whole cell volumes and terminal points suggest that the microglia were in their activated state in frontal cortex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the morphological data on microglia.

claim: There were no significant group differences in astrocyte morphology in either Area 17 or 46.
source: There were no significant group differences in astrocyte morphology in either Area 17 or 46.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data.

claim: In Area 17, the number of cells in which CC3 and SATB2 was colocalized did not differ across the ZIKV-infected and control groups, indicating low frequency of immature neuron death.
source: The number of cells in which CC3 and SATB2 was colocalized did not differ across the ZIKV-infected and control groups and the numbers were fairly low (t4 = 0.65, p = 0.55; d = 0.53; Figure 5A–K), indicating low frequency of immature neuron death.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data and referenced in Figure 5A–K (likely Figure 6A–K based on context).

claim: In Area 46, there was significantly more frequent death of immature neurons in ZIKV-infected compared to control animals, as indicated by a greater number of cells that expressed both CC3 and SATB2.
source: In contrast, there was significantly more frequent death of immature neurons in Area 46 of the ZIKV-infected compared to control animals, as indicated by a greater number of cells that expressed both CC3 and SATB2 (t2.20 = 5.37, p = 0.027; d = 4.39; Figure 6L–Z).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data and referenced in Figure 6L–Z.

claim: Activated microglia (HLA-Dr+) in Area 46 of ZIKV animals present high expression of cell death marker CC3+.
source: Many CC3+ cells in the Area 46 of ZIKV animals are constituted by apoptotic immature neurons, higher resolution 3D analysis showed that activated microglia (HLA-Dr+) also present high expression of cell death marker CC3+ (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from 3D analysis and referenced in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fragmented DNA was observed in Area 46 of ZIKV-infected animals.
source: Fragmented DNA was also observed in this area (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from TUNEL assay and referenced in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The higher frequency of immature neuron death, the active immune response (activated microglia), and the presence of ZIKV protein in Area 46 suggest that frontal cortex remained a site of active ZIKV-induced neuronal remodeling at the time the brains were analyzed.
source: The higher frequency of immature neuron death, the active immune response (activated microglia), and the presence of ZIKV protein in Area 46 suggest that frontal cortex remained a site of active ZIKV-induced neuronal remodeling at the time the brains were analyzed.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple observations including immature neuron death, immune response, and viral protein presence.

claim: Multiple instances of laminar discontinuities within the LGN were observed in the ZIKV-infected subjects.
source: In the ZIKV-infected subjects, we observed multiple instances of laminar discontinuities within the LGN (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from visual inspection of Nissl-stained sections and referenced in Figure 7B–D.

claim: The LGNs of the control subjects were all normal.
source: The LGNs of the control subjects were all normal.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from visual inspection of Nissl-stained sections.

claim: Each ZIKV-infected animal had discrete instances where the koniocellular layer was absent, resulting in indistinct boundaries between layers of the LGN.
source: The first type of LGN pathology consisted of a blurring of the expected boundaries between cell layers. In healthy tissue, the layers of the LGN are separated by a thin layer of koniocellular tissue. However, each ZIKV-infected animal had discrete instances where the koniocellular layer was absent, resulting in indistinct boundaries between layers (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from visual inspection of Nissl-stained sections and referenced in Figure 7B–D.

claim: In the ZIKV-infected animals, there was an increase in the frequency and intensity of the markers for microglia (Iba1) and astrocytes (GFAP) across different layers of the LGN.
source: In comparison to the control animals (Figure 8B–F), in the ZIKV-infected animals, there was an increase in the frequency and intensity of the markers for microglia (Iba1) and astrocytes (GFAP) across different layers of the LGN (Figure 8H–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from fluorescent microscopy and referenced in Figure 8H–L.

claim: No active virus was observed in the LGN region.
source: Although these data suggest the possibility of active inflammatory response occurring, no active virus was observed in this region.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from immunohistochemistry.

claim: Two categories of anatomical abnormalities were identified in the occipital lobe of ZIKV-infected animals (but not controls): laminar disruptions and cortical heterotopias.
source: We identified two categories of anatomical abnormalities in the occipital lobe of ZIKV-infected animals (but not controls): laminar disruptions and cortical heterotopias.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from visual inspection of Nissl-stained sections.

claim: Laminar disruptions were identified within Area 17 and consisted of a break in the continuity of layer 4a.
source: Laminar disruptions were identified within Area 17 and consisted of a break in the continuity of layer 4a (Figure 9A–R).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from visual inspection of Nissl-stained sections and referenced in Figure 9A–R.

claim: The disruption of layer 4a is likely functionally significant, as layer 4a receives direct projections from the LGN.
source: This disruption is likely functionally significant, as layer 4a receives direct projections from the LGN (Thomson and Bannister, 2003; Miller, 2003), and the absence of cells that make up layer 4a likely represent lost visual information.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the known anatomy of the visual system and supported by citations to published research (Thomson and Bannister, 2003; Miller, 2003).

claim: Cortical heterotopias were identified as ectopic islands of neurons extending into cortical layer 1.
source: Cortical heterotopias were identified as ectopic islands of neurons extending into cortical layer 1 (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from visual inspection of Nissl-stained sections and referenced in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: ZIKV infection during fetal development results in central nervous system abnormalities that track with temporal patterns of brain development.
source: Our results demonstrate that ZIKV infection during fetal development results in central nervous system abnormalities that track with temporal patterns of brain development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the overall pattern of results presented in the study.

claim: Virus replication and local neuroinflammatory response were observed in the neocortex of all three ZIKV-infected fetal brains.
source: In the current study, virus replication and local neuroinflammatory response were observed in the neocortex of all three ZIKV-infected fetal brains.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from immunohistochemistry and viral detection.

claim: The types and magnitudes of neuroanatomical abnormalities varied across the cortex, with altered macrostructural features in the occipital cortex and microstructural abnormalities found in the frontal regions of the cortex.
source: The types and magnitudes of these abnormalities varied across the cortex, with altered macrostructural features in the occipital cortex and microstructural abnormalities found in the frontal regions of the cortex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the overall pattern of results presented in the study.

claim: Regional differences in neuroanatomical abnormalities likely reflect the graded manner in which the neocortex develops, with ZIKV infection tracking temporally with neural development.
source: These regional differences likely reflect the graded manner in which the neocortex develops, with ZIKV infection tracking temporally with neural development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pattern of results and knowledge of cortical development.

claim: The neuroanatomical abnormalities observed in all three ZIKV-infected fetal brains occurred even in the absence of microcephaly.
source: Importantly, the neuroanatomical abnormalities that we observed in all three ZIKV-infected fetal brains, but not in control brains, occurred even in the absence of the extreme ZIKV infection phenotype documented in human infants, microcephaly.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing abnormalities without microcephaly.

claim: These findings may help explain why some infants born with normal sized heads during the ZIKV epidemic have developed significant sensory, motor, and sociocognitive challenges as they grow up.
source: These findings may help explain why some infants born with normal sized heads during the ZIKV epidemic have developed significant sensory, motor, and sociocognitive challenges as they grow up (Wheeler et al., 2018; Cardoso et al., 2019; Ventura et al., 2017; Vianna et al., 2018; Marques et al., 2019; Pinato et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the study's findings and supported by citations to published research (Wheeler et al., 2018; Cardoso et al., 2019; Ventura et al., 2017; Vianna et al., 2018; Marques et al., 2019; Pinato et al., 2018).

claim: The neuroanatomical abnormalities appeared to follow the pattern of otherwise normal neuronal development.
source: The neuroanatomical abnormalities that we identified here appeared to follow the pattern of otherwise normal neuronal development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pattern of results.

claim: In mammals the neocortex develops in a gradient, with neural progenitor cells undergoing migration in a caudal-to-rostral pattern.
source: In mammals the neocortex develops in a gradient. Neural progenitor cells undergo migration in a caudal-to-rostral pattern, resulting in occipital regions having mature laminar organization before mature laminar organization is present in frontal regions (Workman et al., 2013; Charvet and Finlay, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Workman et al., 2013; Charvet and Finlay, 2014).

claim: Rhesus monkeys, like humans and NHPs, have frontal cortices that do not reach maturity until well after birth.
source: Rhesus monkeys, like humans and NHPs, have frontal cortices that do not reach maturity until well after birth (Bourgeois et al., 1994; Petanjek et al., 2011; Mrzljak et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Bourgeois et al., 1994; Petanjek et al., 2011; Mrzljak et al., 1991).

claim: Macrostructural differences were observed in the occipital lobe which develops first and microstructural and immune-related differences in frontal lobe which develops later.
source: We observed macrostructural differences (e.g., relative gray/white matter volumes) in the occipital lobe which develops first and microstructural and immune-related differences in frontal lobe which develops later.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the overall pattern of results presented in the study.

claim: Microglia were in their activated state in Area 46 of ZIKV-infected but not control animals, as indicated by smaller whole cell volumes and fewer terminal points.
source: Our analyses revealed evidence that microglia were in their activated state in Area 46 of ZIKV-infected but not control animals, as indicated by smaller whole cell volumes and fewer terminal points.
evidence: The claim is inferred from morphological data on microglia.

claim: Morphological differences in microglia across the groups may be evidence of pathological neuronal development.
source: Microglia play a critical role in neural development via a number of mechanisms (including promoting neuronal survival and removing redundant or dysfunctional synapses) and morphological differences across the groups may be evidence of pathological neuronal development.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the morphological data.

claim: ZIKV-infected fetuses had a greater number of immature cortical neurons undergoing apoptosis compared to control animals.
source: Supporting the idea that ZIKV infection interferes with neural development was our finding that ZIKV-infected fetuses had a greater number of immature cortical neurons undergoing apoptosis compared to control animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from immunohistochemistry.

claim: These differences were found in Area 46, which was still undergoing development at the time of tissue harvest, and not Area 17, which was fully laminated at the time of tissue harvest.
source: That we found these differences in Area 46, which was still undergoing development at the time of tissue harvest, and not Area 17, which was fully laminated at the time of tissue harvest, underscores the ability of ZIKV to interfere with normative neural development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pattern of results.

claim: At the point at which the tissue was harvested, damage had already been done to the part of the brain that was differentiated but the processes of damage were underway in the tissue that was actively developing.
source: One interpretation of these data is that at the point at which the tissue was harvested, damage had already been done to the part of the brain that was differentiated but the processes of damage were underway in the tissue that was actively developing.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the pattern of results.

claim: Infants infected with ZIKV during fetal development and born with normal sized brains may have neurodevelopmental abnormalities that only become apparent later in development.
source: These results suggest that infants infected with ZIKV during fetal development and born with normal sized brains may have neurodevelopmental abnormalities that only become apparent later in development.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the study's findings.

claim: Most infants born during the 2015–2016 ZIKV epidemic in the ZIKV hotspots were born with normal sized heads and microcephaly is thought to be relatively low frequency.
source: This finding is of particular importance because most infants born during the 2015–2016 ZIKV epidemic in the ZIKV hotspots were born with normal sized heads and microcephaly, while an extreme phenotype, is thought to be relatively low frequency (Cardoso et al., 2019; Aragao et al., 2017; Faiçal et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Cardoso et al., 2019; Aragao et al., 2017; Faiçal et al., 2019).

claim: One seemingly consistent anatomical abnormality found in both human patients and animal models of ZIKV is an increased frequency of abnormalities in the visual system.
source: One seemingly consistent anatomical abnormality found in both human patients and animal models of ZIKV is an increased frequency of abnormalities in the visual system (Aleman et al., 2017; Fernandez et al., 2017; Miner et al., 2016b; Simonin et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2018; Ventura et al., 2019; Ventura et al., 2016; Verçosa et al., 2017), especially the retina.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Aleman et al., 2017; Fernandez et al., 2017; Miner et al., 2016b; Simonin et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2018; Ventura et al., 2019; Ventura et al., 2016; Verçosa et al., 2017).

claim: Patients with CZS present with severe eye disease, including congenital cataracts, optic nerve abnormalities, chorioretinal atrophy, intraretinal hemorrhages, mottled retinal pigment epithelium, and blindness.
source: Patients present with severe eye disease, including congenital cataracts, optic nerve abnormalities, chorioretinal atrophy, intraretinal hemorrhages, mottled retinal pigment epithelium, and blindness (Ventura et al., 2017; Aleman et al., 2017; Fernandez et al., 2017; Ventura et al., 2019; Ventura et al., 2016; Verçosa et al., 2017; Miner et al., 2016a; Ventura et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Ventura et al., 2017; Aleman et al., 2017; Fernandez et al., 2017; Ventura et al., 2019; Ventura et al., 2016; Verçosa et al., 2017; Miner et al., 2016a; Ventura et al., 2018).

claim: There is some evidence that ZIKV can be transmitted from the retina to the rest of the visual system via the optic nerve, although this has yet to be confirmed in humans or NHPs.
source: Further, there is some evidence that ZIKV can be transmitted from the retina to the rest of the visual system via the optic nerve, although this has yet to be confirmed in humans or NHPs (van den Pol et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (van den Pol et al., 2017).

claim: Anatomical abnormalities observed in the LGN and Area 17/V1 are consistent with infection and developmental disruption of the eye and optic nerve.
source: Anatomical abnormalities that we observed in the LGN and Area 17/V1 are consistent with infection and developmental disruption of the eye and optic nerve, insofar as projections from the retina enervate the LGN in a retinotopic manner, and projections from the LGN in turn enervate the primary visual cortex (Brodmann's Area 17) (Shatz, 2018; Rakic, 1977).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pattern of results and supported by citations to published research (Shatz, 2018; Rakic, 1977).

claim: The anatomical and functional retinotopic organization of both LGN and V1 is dependent upon activity during developmental critical periods.
source: The anatomical and functional retinotopic organization of both LGN and V1 is dependent upon activity during developmental critical periods (LeVay et al., 1980; Ghosh and Shatz, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (LeVay et al., 1980; Ghosh and Shatz, 1994).

claim: Insults during early development that disrupt activity can result in damage to brain regions downstream of the initial insult.
source: Insults during early development that disrupt this activity can result in damage to brain regions downstream of the initial insult (Ito et al., 2008; Eysel and Wolfhard, 1984; Yücel et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Ito et al., 2008; Eysel and Wolfhard, 1984; Yücel et al., 2003).

claim: The lesions and laminar dysregulations observed in the LGN and V1, respectively, have significant functional consequences.
source: The lesions and laminar dysregulations observed in the LGN and V1, respectively, have significant functional consequences.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the known anatomy and function of the visual system.

claim: Routine H&E histopathology of the eyes did not reveal any significant lesions in these animals.
source: While routine H&E histopathology of the eyes did not reveal any significant lesions in these animals (Coffey et al., 2018), subsequent work from our group has identified retinal pathology in one infant that was infected with ZIKV IA as a fetus and monitored for 2 years after birth (Yiu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Coffey et al., 2018).

claim: Subsequent work identified retinal pathology in one infant that was infected with ZIKV IA as a fetus and monitored for 2 years after birth.
source: While routine H&E histopathology of the eyes did not reveal any significant lesions in these animals (Coffey et al., 2018), subsequent work from our group has identified retinal pathology in one infant that was infected with ZIKV IA as a fetus and monitored for 2 years after birth (Yiu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Yiu et al., 2020).

claim: The retinotopic organization and activity-dependent development of LGN layers suggests that the dysregulation observed within the LGN is likely related to lesions of the retina caused by the Zika virus.
source: However, the retinotopic organization and activity-dependent development of LGN layers suggests that the dysregulation we see within the LGN is likely related to lesions of the retina caused by the Zika virus.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the pattern of results and knowledge of visual system development.

claim: All three infected subjects showed the same pattern of pathology: active inflammation in the still-developing regions of the frontal cortex paired with anatomical abnormalities in the already-developed regions of the caudal cortex.
source: While our sample size was small (N = 3 in each group), only one hemisphere of the brain was available for our analyses, and the timing of ZIKV infection varied across animals (with one ZIKV and one procedure-matched control at each of three infection dates, GD 50, 64, or 90), all three infected subjects showed the same pattern of pathology: active inflammation in the still-developing regions of the frontal cortex paired with anatomical abnormalities in the already-developed regions of the caudal cortex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the overall pattern of results presented in the study.

claim: Each infected fetus had evidence of active virus replication as late as 105-day postinoculation, which could explain the ongoing neurologic damage.
source: Additionally, each infected fetus had evidence of active virus replication as late as 105-day postinoculation, which could explain the ongoing neurologic damage.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from viral detection and is speculative regarding the explanation.

claim: Previous studies have identified discrete histopathological abnormalities in the brain tissue of macaque fetuses infected with ZIKV, including calcifications with gliosis and a loss of neural precursor cells.
source: Previous studies from our group (Coffey et al., 2018) and others (Adams Waldorf et al., 2018; Martinot et al., 2018; Mohr et al., 2018; Steinbach et al., 2020) have identified discrete histopathological abnormalities in the brain tissue of macaque fetuses infected with ZIKV, including calcifications with gliosis and a loss of neural precursor cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Coffey et al., 2018; Adams Waldorf et al., 2018; Martinot et al., 2018; Mohr et al., 2018; Steinbach et al., 2020).

claim: Previous evaluation of the other hemisphere of each of these brains identified ZIKV RNA in Area 46 in all infected animals, and in occipital pole (Area 17) of animals infected at GD 64 and 90.
source: In addition to previous neuropathological evaluations, previous evaluation of the other hemisphere of each of these brains identified ZIKV RNA in Area 46 in all infected animals, and in occipital pole (Area 17) of animals infected at GD 64 and 90 (Coffey et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Coffey et al., 2018).

claim: These analyses paint a picture of inflammatory processes related to viral infiltration sweeping through the cortex and a wave of cell death.
source: Together, these analyses paint a picture of inflammatory processes related to viral infiltration sweeping through the cortex and a wave of cell death.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the overall pattern of results presented in the study.

claim: It is not possible to tell whether inflammatory processes are caused by or are causing cell death, but they certainly appear to co-occur given their proximity.
source: Given our analyses, it is not possible to tell whether inflammatory processes are caused by or are causing cell death, but they certainly appear to co-occur given their proximity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pattern of results.

claim: These findings underscore the importance of adopting quantitative neuroanatomical analyses to understand viral infections of the developing brain.
source: Importantly, in addition to underscoring the importance of adopting quantitative neuroanatomical analyses to understand viral infections of the developing brain, these findings underscore the importance of using a monkey model because we would not expect to see such patterns in nonprimate models, given that rodents do not have a homolog of Area 46 and a significant period of their brain development occurs after birth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the study's approach and findings.

claim: These findings underscore the importance of using a monkey model because rodents do not have a homolog of Area 46 and a significant period of their brain development occurs after birth.
source: Importantly, in addition to underscoring the importance of adopting quantitative neuroanatomical analyses to understand viral infections of the developing brain, these findings underscore the importance of using a monkey model because we would not expect to see such patterns in nonprimate models, given that rodents do not have a homolog of Area 46 and a significant period of their brain development occurs after birth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the study's approach and findings, drawing on knowledge of comparative neuroanatomy.

claim: Rhesus monkeys are a robust model for human infant development across a variety of behavioral domains – including cognition, affect, and social behavior.
source: Rhesus monkeys are a robust model for human infant development across a variety of behavioral domains – including cognition, affect, and social behavior (Phillips et al., 2014; Clancy et al., 2013; Fox, 1984; Cassidy and Shaver, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Phillips et al., 2014; Clancy et al., 2013; Fox, 1984; Cassidy and Shaver, 1999).

claim: Rhesus monkeys develop three to four times faster than humans.
source: Because rhesus monkeys develop three to four times faster than humans (Workman et al., 2013), a separate, currently ongoing cohort of infants who were infected with ZIKV as fetuses will soon out-age human infants who were infected in utero, thus providing a prospective look at the challenges those infants may face.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Workman et al., 2013).

claim: Long-term developmental studies have documented significant neural and behavioral plasticity following early brain damage.
source: In this context, our long-term developmental studies which have documented significant neural and behavioral plasticity following early brain damage (e.g., Grayson et al., 2017; Bliss-Moreau et al., 2017) provide hope that fairly simple behavioral interventions may be possible to improve the outcomes for impacted children.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Grayson et al., 2017; Bliss-Moreau et al., 2017).

claim: The ZIKV epidemic disproportionally impacted people of color living in socioeconomically disadvantaged communities.
source: This is particularly important given that the ZIKV epidemic disproportionally impacted people of color living in socioeconomically disadvantaged communities (Moreno-Madriñán et al., 2017; Kapiriri and Ross, 2020; Gómez et al., 2018) and that ZIKV is expected to return seasonally in the future (Tesla et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Moreno-Madriñán et al., 2017; Kapiriri and Ross, 2020; Gómez et al., 2018).
